articles.title: '140 clicks was hard to come by': Ravi Shastri questions India's pace attack, asks 'Where was Siraj?'
articles.summary: Former India head coach Ravi Shastri questioned India's decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the opening Test against New Zealand,
articles.body: Former India head coach Ravi Shastri questioned India's decision to leave Mohammed Siraj out of the playing XI for the opening Test against New Zealand, after the hosts staged a remarkable recovery on Day 1 at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday.India appeared to have seized control of the contest after reducing New Zealand to 70/5, with Jasprit Bumrah leading the charge. However, Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips produced a stunning counterattack, stitching together an unbeaten 173-run partnership to take the hosts to 243/5 at stumps.With India's pace attack struggling to make further inroads after the initial breakthroughs, Siraj's omission became a major talking point among former cricketers and experts.Taking to X after the day's play, Shastri questioned whether India's selection committee had overlooked the experience and aggression that the Hyderabad pacer brings to the bowling attack."Hope India bounce back strongly. But if pace, skill and seam movement were the criteria, and 140 clicks was hard to come by, one has to ask the question. Where was MOHD SIRAJ? Experience, aggression and the ability to make things happen with the ball. Surely that counts for something!" Shastri wrote.India batting coach defends Siraj's omissionMeanwhile, India batting coach Sitanshu Kotak defended the team management's decision, insisting that the playing XI was selected keeping the entire five-day contest in mind rather than just the opening day.Kotak maintained that there was nothing wrong with Siraj and backed the combination chosen for the Wellington Test."There is nothing wrong with Siraj. We thought this was the best XI when we picked the side. I don't think dropping Siraj was a wrong decision. This is just the first day. We don't pick a team only for day one, but also for days two, three and four," Kotak said.India vs New Zealand, 1st Test: Day 1 reportEarlier in the day, India enjoyed a commanding start after winning the toss and opting to bowl. Bumrah struck with the third delivery of the match, dismissing New Zealand captain Tom Latham for a duck. The visitors continued to exploit the early assistance on offer, with Akash Deep and Bumrah among the wickets as New Zealand struggled to negotiate the movement and bounce.Rachin Ravindra and Daryl Mitchell also departed cheaply, while Bumrah removed Tom Blundell shortly after lunch to leave the hosts reeling at 70/5. However, Nicholls and Phillips turned the contest around with a magnificent partnership. Nicholls remained unbeaten on 113 off 221 deliveries, striking 14 boundaries, while Phillips finished the day on 94 not out off 182 balls, with 13 fours.The duo added 173 runs without being separated, taking New Zealand to 243/5 after 82 overs at stumps on Day 1.Bumrah was India's standout bowler with three wickets, while Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj picked up one apiece. Prasidh Krishna, however, went wicketless as the hosts wrested back control of the contest.With Phillips just six runs short of his century and Nicholls well-set at the other end, India will need early breakthroughs on Day 2 to prevent New Zealand from building a substantial first-innings total.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Record! Yuzvendra Chahal becomes first Indian bowler to cross historic milestone
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Yuzvendra Chahal has created history in Indian cricket by becoming the first Indian bowler to take 400 wickets in T20 cricket.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Yuzvendra Chahal has created history in Indian cricket by becoming the first Indian bowler to take 400 wickets in T20 cricket.He achieved this milestone on Wednesday while playing for Haryana against Tamil Nadu in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2026-27.The 36-year-old leg-spinner needed just one wicket to reach the landmark but ended up taking three. He finished with impressive figures of 3 wickets for 16 runs in four overs, helping Haryana bowl out Tamil Nadu for just 124 runs in 19.5 overs.With this performance, Chahal's total T20 wicket tally reached 402 in 246 matches.India's leading T20 wicket-takerChahal now stands ahead of some of India's biggest bowling names. Bhuvneshwar Kumar is second on the list with 366 wickets, followed by Jasprit Bumrah with 354. Piyush Chawla and Ravichandran Ashwin occupy the next two spots with 329 and 323 wickets respectively.Although Chahal has not played for the Indian national team since 2023, he has continued to perform well in domestic tournaments and franchise cricket.He has represented several IPL teams, including Royal Challengers Bengaluru and Rajasthan Royals. He currently plays for Punjab Kings, who signed him for Rs 18 crore ahead of the 2025 season.Among the world's bestOn the global T20 wicket-taking list, Afghanistan's Rashid Khan leads with 743 wickets in 553 matches.West Indies spinner Sunil Narine is second with 658 wickets, while former West Indies all-rounder Dwayne Bravo is third with 631 wickets.With 402 wickets to his name, Chahal has now reached a special milestone and strengthened his position as one of India's most successful T20 bowlers.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: South Africa maintain No.1 Test ranking after nine-wicket win over Bangladesh, take 1-0 series lead
articles.summary: South Africa continued their dominance in Test cricket, underlining why they sit at the summit of the ICC Men's Test Team Rankings with a commanding
articles.body: South Africa continued their dominance in Test cricket, underlining why they sit at the summit of the ICC Men's Test Team Rankings with a commanding nine-wicket victory over Bangladesh in the opening Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg on Thursday. Simon Harmer produced a match-winning spell to dismantle Bangladesh's lower order as the reigning World Test champions wrapped up the contest inside the opening session on Day 5.The Proteas, who dethroned Australia from the No. 1 position following their memorable 2-1 Test series triumph last month, carried that momentum into their home series against Bangladesh. The victory also gave Temba Bavuma's side a 1-0 lead in the two-match series.Simon Harmer spins South Africa to victoryResuming Day 5 at 100/5 in their second innings, Bangladesh needed a substantial lower-order contribution to put South Africa under pressure. However, Harmer had other plans as the off-spinner ran through the visitors' batting line-up.After Kagiso Rabada dismissed Litton Das for 39, Harmer picked up four of the remaining five wickets to bowl Bangladesh out for 168. He finished with figures of 6/51, while Rabada claimed 3/48. Harmer once again proved instrumental in South Africa's success, bringing back memories of his sensational 6/16 spell on the final day of the series-clinching victory over Australia last month.South Africa needed just 12 runs to complete the victory and lost Marques Ackerman, who had scored a magnificent 157 in the first innings, for a second-ball duck. Aiden Markram survived a brief scare after being bowled off a no-ball by Ebadot Hossain before scoring the winning run to take South Africa to 12/1. The hosts eventually sealed a nine-wicket victory before lunch.South Africa's batting dominance sets up comfortable victoryEarlier, Bangladesh had posted a competitive 400 in their first innings, with Litton Das leading the charge through a brilliant 120. However, South Africa responded with an imposing 557, taking a crucial 157-run first-innings lead. Ackerman starred with a maiden Test century, smashing 157 off 164 deliveries, while Zubayr Hamza contributed 83 and Ryan Rickelton scored 102.Bangladesh struggled to build on their first-innings effort in the second innings, eventually folding for 168 as South Africa's bowlers took control of the contest. The result leaves South Africa firmly in control of the series, with the second and final Test scheduled to be played in Centurion from November 23 to 27.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: South Africa vs Bangladesh: Simon Harmer stars as Proteas seal nine-wicket first Test win
articles.summary: South Africa edged closer to securing a spot in the World Test Championship final with a nine-wicket victory against Bangladesh on Thursday; Simon Harmer took four wickets to bowl out Bangladesh; watch the second Test live on Sky Sports Cricket
articles.body:
The win sees the Proteas edge closer to securing a spot at the World Test Championship final at The Kia Oval in 2027, with the defending champions having dethroned Australia to go top of the ICC rankings following their series win last month.

Resuming on 100-5 at the Wanderers, Bangladesh's lower-order batters couldn't handle the off-spin of Harmer, who took four of the remaining five wickets to help dismiss the tourists for 168 and return figures of 6-51.

It revived memories of Harmer taking 6-16 on day five of the series-clinching victory over Australia last month.

"I don't think I bowled my best this match," Harmer told SuperSport .

"But I'm very aware of the way cricket works; you're going to have days where you bowl well and don't necessarily get rewards.

"Sometimes you don't bowl as well as you should, but you end up getting wickets.

"It would have been tricky if we were chasing 150 or 170. To be able to restrict them and get wickets in the third innings is enjoyable and it's always nice to contribute."

There is bad news for South Africa, though, who are likely to be without their captain Temba Bavuma for the second Test, live on Sky Sports , with the skipper still struggling to overcome a fitness issue.

The Proteas lost first-innings century-maker Marques Ackerman - for a second-ball duck - on the way to reaching their target before lunch at 12-1. Soon after getting bowled off a no-ball, Aiden Markram (8 not out) scored the winning run.

In Harmer, South Africa have a 37-year-old player enjoying a renaissance in a Test career that was drifting until a year ago, when he returned after a two-and-a-half-year absence. He is now a reliable match-winner.

Having already removed Najmul Hossain Shanto and Mahfijul Islam late on day four, Harmer took the final four wickets of the match in his brilliant four-over burst that came after overnight batter Litton Das got an inside edge and played onto his own stumps off Kagiso Rabada (3-46).

Mushfiqur Rahim added 34 runs to his overnight five before gloving Harmer to a close fielder, for a dismissal that was only given after the Proteas reviewed a not-out call.

In his next over, Harmer had Mehidy Hasan Miraz stumped for four before removing Hasan Mahmud (4) and Ebadot Hossain (0) in consecutive balls to wrap up the innings.

Despite making 400 in the first innings after winning the toss, Bangladesh barely avoided an innings defeat.

articles.title: 'Pakistan used bottle tops, not sandpaper': Shoaib Akhtar asks people to stop 'making fuss' over Khawaja's claims
articles.summary: The ball-tampering controversy that shook Australian cricket in 2018 has returned to the spotlight after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja made fresh
articles.body: The ball-tampering controversy that shook Australian cricket in 2018 has returned to the spotlight after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja made fresh revelations in his autobiography, Sabr.Pakistan fast-bowling legend Shoaib Akhtar has now reacted to the claims, admitting that ball-tampering was not limited to Australia and revealing that Pakistan players also used different methods during his playing days.The controversy, popularly known as Sandpapergate, began during the 2018 Test between Australia and South Africa in Cape Town. Cameron Bancroft was caught on camera using sandpaper on the ball. An investigation by Cricket Australia followed, resulting in suspensions for Bancroft, David Warner and then captain Steve Smith.Years later, Khawaja's book has brought the issue back into discussion. He claimed that the entire Australian team knew about the incident and that only three players were punished. While current Australia captain Pat Cummins rejected his claims, Bancroft and Warner have also spoken in support of Khawaja's version.Akhtar admits Pakistan also tampered with the ballReacting to the controversy, Akhtar said people should stop making a big issue out of the matter. He also criticised Khawaja for speaking about his former teammates, saying that he had his own disagreements with past teammates but would not publicly expose them."Mate, come on. Let go of it now. Why are you making a huge fuss out of this? I understand it's damage to cricket. It damaged our cricket too. We used to use bottle tops, not sandpaper, back in England. We used to change the balls and do all sorts of things. I mean, okay, you come out with the truth and that's about it, but don't make a fuss about it," Akhtar told Wisden.'It has to be a team decision'Akhtar also agreed with Khawaja's suggestion that the Australian team knew about the ball-tampering incident. According to the former Pakistan pacer, such actions could not happen without the knowledge of the entire team."The thing is, what Usman said, it has to be a team decision. It cannot be a couple of guys' decision. I'm sorry to say this. We used to play with cricket balls. I did all sorts of things, right? But the whole team knew it because if we didn't reverse the ball, we weren't going to win games. Now, what is coming out is absolute chaos. But it shouldn't have happened. He did the right thing, but the timing could have been better than this," Akhtar added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sandpapergate: Michael Atherton believes Pat Cummins won't resign as Australia captain despite Cameron Bancroft's explosive claims
articles.summary: Pat Cummins is facing scrutiny over his role as Australia's Test cricket captain following his denials of Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft's claims that the entire Australian cricket team knew about ball tampering during Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa
articles.body:
Cummins is facing scrutiny for his denials of both Usman Khawaja and Cameron Bancroft's claims that the entire Australian team knew ball tampering was taking place during their 2018 tour of South Africa.

The Australia captain dismissed Khawaja's claims during a press conference on November 13, saying they were "100 per cent wrong", but Bancroft later issued a 4,000-word statement supporting the allegations, adding Cummins' denials left him "angry, betrayed and alone".

Cummins' management have issued multiple statements since , saying there was "nothing in the [Bancroft's] statement that hasn't been answered" and later adding that he has been "consistent and adamant" from day one .

He is facing calls to resign but when asked if he believes Cummins' position is untenable, Atherton told the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast that he believes there is no "immediate threat" to the bowler's role as Australia's Test captain.

"I don't think so, yet," Atherton said. "A few things are obvious. One, he has the support of Cricket Australia. David Boone [Cricket Australia interim chair], about a week ago, was very clear about that. On Wednesday, Boone and [Cricket Australia chief executive, Todd] Greenberg reiterated that very strongly.

"He's obviously got a lot of credit in the bank in terms of performance as captain, having transformed the culture and kept Australia at the top of the tree, if you like.

"So I don't think there's an immediate threat there."

Atherton added that public reaction to Cummins' comments will be "important" in the discussion.

"He [Cummins] is very much the 'blue-eyed boy' of Australian cricket, isn't he? He's been that way ever since he came into the team," Atherton said.

"Obviously [he] is a great bowler and a top-class captain now.

"But the public reaction will be interesting because the sympathy now is almost going towards the lads who took the fall, particularly Bancroft.

"If the sympathy moves that way, it'll move against the others who are in the other camp, of which Cummins is one. That public reaction will be interesting. It will probably be important.

"Organisations are pretty fickle, aren't they? They support you until you don't. If the public turn on you, that can be a different thing.

"I don't know what he said today, but they, the cameras, were chasing him today.

"It's very much that kind of febrile atmosphere at the moment."

Atherton added: "That gives a sense of crisis, doesn't it? But I don't know. Maybe I'm wrong, but I don't see that [his resignation] happening immediately."

'There was clearly a toxic dressing-room culture'

Bancroft, who was banned for nine months after the saga, also delved into discussions about the use of sandpaper in the Australian dressing room during the tour of South Africa, claiming the side was also using sandpaper in the second Test in Port Elizabeth as well as the third Test in Cape Town.

Bancroft said he recalled conversations with Australia's pacers, Cummins, Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about "whether it was swinging enough", and that all players and coaches were present when media manager Kate Hutchinson expressed her opposition to the plans.

"There is still some doubt about exactly who knew what," Atherton said, when asked if he had sympathy for Bancroft.

"It seems to me that two things are absolutely clear. One is the build-up to it. And I've read Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr .

"It's a very interesting book in a broader sense than just the sandpaper stuff. But reading his book, reading what Cameron Bancroft said in that 4,000-word statement, it's clear that [there was in] the build-up to the South Africa tour, this almost institutional pressure that was put on the team, this win-at-all-costs mentality, is how they phrased it.

"In fact, Todd Greenberg, the chief executive of Cricket Australia, did say that Cricket Australia bore some accountability and responsibility for that.

"It was a build-up of pressure. And that was the dressing room that Cameron Bancroft walked into. If you remember, he made his debut in the 2017 Ashes series, the first Test of that series in Brisbane.

"His 4,000-word statement actually starts there, because he said, you need to know the context of the dressing room I was walking into. And it was clearly a team with a toxic dressing room culture at that point.

"That had been building up, and that's background to South Africa. That seems to me a really important part of this story."

'Public cannot accept how they allowed three players to take the rap'

Reflecting on events that unfolded in the wake of the saga, Atherton added: "As we say, more than three players must have known and yet the team let those three players carry the can and take the rap.

"That seems to me incredible. So those two aspects are the things that have made this story."

He added: "It's that the context of the build-up to it and the toxic dressing-room culture meant Cricket Australia would hand down heavier sanctions, that there'd be an ethics committee, an ethics investigation, and the whole thing blew up in that sense.

"And then what happened afterwards, the public, I think, cannot take the fact that they allowed three players to take the rap. That's a very long answer to your original question, I think, which was, do you have sympathy for Bancroft?

"And the sympathy is that he was a young kid who was one of three who were allowed to take the rap when clearly there was a broader knowledge there."

articles.title: England cricket: Harry Brook and Tom Banton are bowling options for World Cup, says Brendon McCullum
articles.summary: England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum believes that batters Harry Brook and Tom Banton can be genuine bowling options as they prepare for next year's World Cup.
articles.body:
England white-ball coach Brendon McCullum plans to use batters Tom Banton and Harry Brook as spin-bowling options in the one-day international (ODI) side.

McCullum and captain Brook, 27, are preparing England for next year's 50-over World Cup, which takes place in southern Africa.

It has been a winter of mixed performances for the side, who suffered disappointing defeats by Pakistan and Sri Lanka in the tri-series before an impressive 2-1 series win in Australia .

With the World Cup taking place across different venues in South Africa, Namibia and Zimbabwe, McCullum referenced the need to develop the duo as part-time bowlers in potentially contrasting conditions.

"These guys are talented, there is something there," said McCullum.

"We are looking at a World Cup in 12 months' time, and no one knows what the conditions are going to be like. You could end up on a pitch that is exploding and need some options.

"We will keep encouraging them to do that. That World Cup is potentially 13 games in three different countries, fresh pitches, there's not much data on how those pitches will play, no one really knows.

"It's like your bowlers - you encourage them to practise batting, because we have seen the likes of Gus Atkinson, how valuable his runs have been for us."

In recent games, McCullum has opted for one frontline spinner in England's XI and left-armer Liam Dawson has been preferred over veteran leg-spinner Adil Rashid.

Will Jacks and Joe Root have been used as part-timers, which is a role that Jacob Bethell would also be likely to fulfil if selected after he recovers from a knee injury .

Brook has occasionally bowled medium-pace in Tests, but bowled for the first time in his ODI career in England's win at Hobart on Wednesday, taking the final wicket of Spencer Johnson with his new style of off-spin.

Banton, who is also a wicketkeeper, bowled in England's warm-up game against Western Australia in Perth and claimed the wicket of former Australia all-rounder Ashton Agar.

McCullum made the comparison to spin-bowling all-rounders from his native New Zealand, Glenn Phillips and Michael Bracewell, who are also wicketkeepers by trade but have established themselves as spinners in all formats after experimenting in training.

England are likely to need that flexibility for the World Cup, where only 15 players are allowed in a squad.

Their tour of Australia continues with five T20s, the first of which takes place at the Melbourne Cricket Ground on Saturday.

articles.summary: South Africa's bid to complete a series whitewash against Bangladesh has suffered a setback, with captain Temba Bavuma ruled out of the second and final
articles.body: South Africa's bid to complete a series whitewash against Bangladesh has suffered a setback, with captain Temba Bavuma ruled out of the second and final Test due to a calf injury. The Proteas skipper sustained a strain during the opening Test at the Wanderers in Johannesburg and will miss the upcoming clash in Centurion, starting Monday.The injury comes at an important stage for South Africa, who are looking to build on their commanding nine-wicket victory in the series opener and strengthen their position at the top of the World Test Championship (WTC) standings. With Bavuma unavailable, Aiden Markram is likely to take over the captaincy for the final fixture.Bavuma sustains calf injury during first Test against BangladeshBavuma picked up the injury during South Africa's first innings in Johannesburg, forcing him to retire hurt on 49. However, the right-handed batter returned to the crease after the hosts lost their eighth wicket and continued his innings.He eventually finished unbeaten on 68, playing a crucial role in South Africa's recovery alongside the lower order. Bavuma added 19 runs with Kagiso Rabada for the ninth wicket before sharing another valuable 45-run stand with Dane Paterson as the Proteas reached 557, securing a significant 157-run first-innings lead.Despite appearing comfortable while batting, Bavuma did not take the field during Bangladesh's second innings.Cricket South Africa subsequently confirmed the extent of the injury, stating that scans had revealed a strain in his right calf."Subsequent scans have confirmed that Temba Bavuma has sustained a right calf strain. He will not take to the field in the second innings but will bat if required," CSA said in a statement.Aiden Markram likely to captain South Africa in Bavuma's absenceWith Bavuma unavailable for the series finale, Markram is expected to lead the Proteas in Centurion. South Africa will nevertheless enter the contest with considerable confidence after their dominant performance in the opening Test. Simon Harmer's six-wicket haul helped bowl Bangladesh out for 168 in their second innings, leaving the hosts with a modest target of 12 runs, which they chased down for a nine-wicket victory.Speaking after the win, Bavuma offered an update on his fitness but acknowledged that he would need to manage the injury over the coming weeks."Could be better. articles.summary: The Proteas South Africa moved past New Zealand to claim the No.1 position, taking their points percentage (PCT) to 75 per cent after their latest triumph
articles.body: The Proteas South Africa moved past New Zealand to claim the No.1 position, taking their points percentage (PCT) to 75 per cent after their latest triumph against Bangladesh. The Black Caps, who are currently involved in a two-match Test series against India, slipped to second place with 72.22 per cent.Meanwhile, India remain fourth in the standings with a PCT of 51.52 per cent, leaving them with plenty of ground to cover if they are to secure a place in a third consecutive WTC final after finishing runners-up in the 2021 and 2023 editions.South Africa dethrone New Zealand to take No.1 spotSouth Africa's rise to the top comes on the back of an impressive run in Test cricket. The reigning world champions had already moved from third to second following their memorable 2-1 series victory over Australia at home.Before the opening Test against Bangladesh, Temba Bavuma's side were placed second with a PCT of 71.43 per cent, behind New Zealand's 72.22 per cent and ahead of Australia's 69.23 per cent.However, the nine-wicket victory in Johannesburg lifted South Africa's PCT to 75 per cent, taking them past the Black Caps and establishing them as the current table-toppers in the WTC 2025-27 cycle.New Zealand, meanwhile, remain second with 72.22 per cent and will have an opportunity to strengthen their position in the ongoing Test series against India.Where does India stand in the WTC 2025-27 points table?India occupy fourth place with a PCT of 51.52 per cent, considerably behind the top three teams in the championship standings.The Indian team have finished as runners-up in the first two WTC finals, losing to New Zealand in 2021 and Australia in 2023. They will be determined to avoid another near miss and return to the summit clash in the ongoing cycle.However, with South Africa and New Zealand currently enjoying a healthy lead over them, India will need consistent results in their remaining fixtures to improve their chances of qualification. Their ongoing two-match Test series against New Zealand presents an important opportunity to collect valuable WTC points and close the gap on the teams above them.Bangladesh slip further down after Johannesburg defeatBangladesh's defeat against South Africa has further dented their position in the WTC standings. Before the opening Test, the Tigers had a PCT of 45.83 per cent, but the nine-wicket loss brought it down to 40.74 per cent. articles.title: Sandpapergate: Pat Cummins' Australia captaincy at a crossroads - Agnew
articles.summary: Jonathan Agnew says he struggles to see how Pat Cummins can lead Australia into next summer's Ashes series in England following latest developments in the sandpapergate scandal.
articles.body:
Australia captain Pat Cummins, much like his fellow bowlers, is in the eye of the sandpapergate storm at the moment.

The reason is simple to me. The very notion that Cameron Bancroft - the most inexperienced batsman in the Australia team at the time – would use sandpaper on the ball against South Africa without the bowlers knowing has never made sense.

It has never seemed remotely plausible to me, as a former bowler, that the bowlers didn't know what was happening in Cape Town in 2018. It just doesn't seem possible.

Therefore, this day of reckoning was always going to come.

Let's be clear - as long as there has been cricket, there has been ball-tampering. There is no point hiding from the fact.

Back in the day it was about shining the ball, maybe using something like a sweet to get a sheen on one side.

Reverse swing was a ball-tampering game-changer. There was a requirement for a wearing process, roughing up and drying the ball.

But, to get one thing straight, whether a ball is being tampered with or not, it belongs to the bowlers. It is the bowling attack's weapon. As much as a bowler would not fiddle with a batsman's bat – sanding an edge or changing the grip - a batsman would not work on the ball without the knowledge of a bowler.

Some might wonder why revelations relating to the sandpaper controversy have not come to light before.

In response to that, I would say it would have been very difficult for a player in the Australia team to go public at the time. They would have been worried about their own futures, their careers.

Only when a player has retired, or believe their time as an international cricketer has come to an end, do they feel more comfortable to speak up.

I have also seen suggestions that Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner have had their guilt diminished by what has emerged in recent days, that they took bullets for their team-mates.

Smith was captain and should have been in control of his team. Warner cooked up the sandpaper idea. Bancroft executed it. If they did take bullets, they were bullets they deserved.

Now, the spotlight has fallen on Pat Cummins, whose agent has repeated his client's version of events in the last 24 hours.

The junior bowler at the time, Cummins has ascended to the captaincy, often joked to be the second-most important job in Australia, behind only the prime minister.

Cummins is not a typical Australian captain. He is not abrasive, or in your face. When he says he has worked hard to correct the image of his team, he is credible. Then again, he missed a trick to really prove Australia are no longer a win-at-all-costs outfit with the Jonny Bairstow stumping in the 2023 Ashes Test at Lord's.

After everything he said in public, and the way he has been backed by Cricket Australia (CA), there seems to be no obvious suggestion Cummins has considered resigning, or that he will be sacked.

He is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand in Perth on 9 December.

Looking ahead to that match, it is difficult to see how the build-up will be anything other than a circus, dominated by questions about sandpaper, who knew what and who said what to whom.

The litmus test for Cummins will be the public reaction. Remember, that Test is being played in Bancroft's home city, in the state of the newspaper where his 4,000-word testimony was first published.

If Cummins is still in his position by then, the response of the Perth crowd to the captain will be very interesting.

Even if Cummins does get through that, the Australian media will not let up. This is a huge story, one of the biggest in the history of Australia sport. The press will bang away until they feel they have got the truth.

And what about next summer's Ashes? If Cummins is tossing the coin at Trent Bridge on 18 June, then he is extraordinarily resilient.

Right now, I can't imagine that happening. He has said he never wants to talk about sandpaper again, which is ludicrous when you think what he will face on that tour: scrutiny from the media, constant baiting from the crowds.

Cummins will have to decide if he has the stomach for all of that, and whether he can see it through.

His way out could be to resign, without admitting guilt. To say the speculation has become a distraction for the team and the pressure is taking a toll on his family life – we have seen more pictures from Australia overnight of Cummins being confronted outside his home.

Cummins could perhaps continue in the ranks, just as Warner and Smith did. A resignation without an admission of guilt may also take the heat off the other bowlers – Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon.

Whether Cummins continues or not, questions will remain for others who were in Cape Town, Cricket Australia and the whole culture of the sport in that country.

Looking now at what happened in 2018, it appears there was an attitude in the Australia camp that they were fireproof, that they could get away with anything.

Credit goes to their media manager Kate Hutchison, who, according to Bancroft, made a stand about what was going on and knew what would happen if and when the Aussies got caught.

What about the others involved, coaches who were supposed to guide and protect young men? Darren Lehmann and his position at Northamptonshire, or David Saker, who has recently been working with England.

Cricket Australia has seemed so reluctant to get involved. If the big idea was to give individuals the opportunity to "tell their truth" behind closed doors, it is surely dead in the water.

What about telling THE truth? Nothing else is good enough.

articles.title: 'Give young players a solid run': Smriti Mandhana gets Mithali Raj's advice ahead of India's South Africa tour
articles.summary: Former India captain Mithali Raj has advised women's team skipper Smriti Mandhana to give young players enough opportunities to prove themselves ahead of
articles.body: Former India captain Mithali Raj has advised women's team skipper Smriti Mandhana to give young players enough opportunities to prove themselves ahead of India's all-format tour of South Africa, starting December 9. Mithali believes youngsters should not be judged based on just one or two matches, as regular opportunities at the international level help them gain confidence and experience.Speaking to ANI at an event in Mumbai, Mithali pointed out that players coming through the Women's Premier League (WPL) have already gained valuable exposure.She also stressed that playing against teams of different strengths helps youngsters prepare for bigger challenges."When you select young players, it is important to give them a solid run. You cannot judge them from a match or two. When youngsters are given chances, especially in T20Is, like Anushka Sharma and Niki Prasad, they have got experience from the Women's Premier League; it will benefit them. Even though Zimbabwe is a lower-ranked team," she said."Experience is experience. The environment in an international match is different, so I think that whatever experience they get from their matches, it will help them against South Africa or in South Africa," she added.Young players getting opportunitiesIndia have included several youngsters in their squads for the South Africa tour, including Niki Prasad, Anushka Sharma, Prema Rawat and Nandani Sharma, who have made their international debuts this year.Niki impressed during the T20I series against Zimbabwe, scoring 48 runs in two innings and picking up three wickets. Prema has taken seven wickets in seven matches, while Anushka has scored 105 runs in six appearances.India will play one Test, three ODIs and three T20Is during the tour. The Test will begin in Gqeberha on December 9, followed by the ODI series from December 16. The three-match T20I series will start on December 26.Smriti Mandhana will lead India across all three formats. Deepti Sharma has been named vice-captain for the Test and ODI squads, while Shafali Verma will serve as vice-captain in T20Is.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Dhoni has a lot more to contribute': Venkatesh Prasad backs former India captain's mentor role after IPL retirement
articles.summary: Mahendra Singh Dhoni may have played his final match in the Indian Premier League, but his association with Chennai Super Kings (CSK) is set to continue
articles.body: Mahendra Singh Dhoni may have played his final match in the Indian Premier League, but his association with Chennai Super Kings (CSK) is set to continue in a new role. Former India pacer Venkatesh Prasad believes the legendary wicketkeeper-batter still has plenty to offer the franchise, particularly through his experience and guidance for its younger players.Dhoni's 18-year IPL journey came to an end on November 17, when CSK officially announced that he would take over as the team's mentor from the 2027 season. The former India captain, who missed the entire IPL 2026 campaign due to a calf injury, will now transition into a mentoring role after an illustrious playing career.Speaking on the sidelines of a tennis event on Thursday, Prasad reflected on Dhoni's contribution to Indian cricket and backed him to continue making an impact away from the field.'He has a lot more to contribute': Prasad on Dhoni's CSK mentor rolePrasad, who has worked closely with Dhoni during his time with the Indian team and in the IPL, described the former captain as a legend whose contribution to Indian cricket across formats has been immense. He also highlighted Dhoni's achievements as captain, including India's triumphs in the 2007 T20 World Cup and 2011 ODI World Cup."He has been a legend who has contributed immensely to Indian cricket in all formats of the game, be it T20Is or ODIs, by winning those World Cups. I have worked with him closely in the IPL and in the Test and ODI formats," Prasad said.The former India bowling coach believes Dhoni's experience will be particularly valuable for CSK's younger players as the franchise enters a new phase."But now, as a mentor of his franchise (CSK) in the IPL, I am sure he has a lot more to contribute to the team and to the youngsters playing in it," he added.Prasad backs Dhoni's decision to retire from IPLPrasad also spoke about the inevitability of retirement, stating that even the greatest players eventually have to step away from the sport. While acknowledging that every cricketer wants to continue playing for as long as possible, he felt Dhoni had reached a stage where moving on from his playing career was understandable after everything he had achieved."His contribution is incredible. Having said that, everybody has to go through this (retirement). Though everybody wants to play as long as they are alive, it is not humanly possible. There comes a time when everybody has to call it a day."It has happened to the greats. There is a shelf life. He must have had enough, and he has gone out on his own terms, after having contributed so much on the field," Prasad said.Dhoni's association with PrasadPrasad also shares a connection with Dhoni through India's successful 2007 campaigns. He was part of the coaching setup as bowling coach when India won a historic Test series in England under Rahul Dravid before Dhoni led the team to the inaugural T20 World Cup title in South Africa later that year.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Meeting PM Modi turned out to be very lucky': Suryakumar Yadav on rediscovering batting form
articles.summary: Suryakumar Yadav believes his meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 6 was a lucky moment for him, as he began scoring runs again after a
articles.body: Suryakumar Yadav believes his meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 6 was a lucky moment for him, as he began scoring runs again after a difficult period.The India batter met the Prime Minister along with his family and said the interaction turned out to be much longer and more memorable than he had expected.Speaking at an event in New Delhi, where he received the Outstanding Achievement Award, Suryakumar recalled the meeting and the conversation he had with Modi."I think that meeting turned out to be very lucky. I started scoring runs again. But it was a very good meeting. We thought, it would be only for five minutes or 10 minutes, but he gave around 40-45 minutes to me and my family. So it was a very beautiful moment," Suryakumar told News18."Spoke to him about how he is handling all the situations. I mean, we play this game, and we feel under pressure, but I asked him how under pressure you are when you are dealing with all the situations. So he answered all the questions very nicely. So, it was a very light moment."Suryakumar's explosive return to formThe 36-year-old has recently found his batting rhythm in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy 2026-27, where he is leading Mumbai. He made an impressive start against Hyderabad, scoring an unbeaten 60 off just 21 balls, including six fours and five sixes.He then smashed 82 off 29 deliveries against Gujarat, helping Mumbai chase down 199 in just 15.4 overs. He also scored a quick 25 against Goa.These performances have come at an important time, as Suryakumar looks to return to India's T20I team. His position came under pressure after a disappointing IPL 2026 season, in which he scored 269 runs in 13 innings. The selectors appointed Shreyas Iyer as India's T20I captain in June.However, Suryakumar had earlier led India to a successful T20 World Cup title defence in 2026, scoring 242 runs in nine innings, including an important 84 against the USA.Eyes set on Mumbai Indians' IPL 2027 titleWhile making a case for his international comeback, Suryakumar also has a clear target for the next IPL season. The Mumbai Indians batter wants to help his franchise lift the trophy in 2027."I want to win the latest IPL tournament, which is coming in 2027, for Mumbai Indians," he added.Suryakumar has been with Mumbai Indians since 2018, having previously represented the franchise in 2012 before spending three seasons with Kolkata Knight Riders.Retained by Mumbai Indians for IPL 2027, he will now hope to continue his strong domestic form and earn another opportunity to represent India in T20Is.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: Temba Bavuma has become the most successful captain in terms of Test wins after leading a team in his first 16 matches. The South Africa skipper registered his 14th victory in the format after his team beat Bangladesh by nine wickets in the first Test at the Wanderers Stadium on Thursday, moving past Australia's Lindsay Hassett, who had won 13 of his first 16 Tests as captain.Simon Harmer wrapped up Bangladesh's tail to complete the victory, but South Africa will be without Bavuma for the second Test, which begins next Monday in Centurion. The captain has been ruled out of the match after sustaining a calf injury while batting in the series opener.South Africa's win also took them to the top of the World Test Championship standings. They have now won six of their eight matches in the current cycle.Most Test wins in first 16 matches as captain14Temba Bavuma13Lindsay Hassett11Bill Woodfull11Steve Waugh11Ricky PontingBavuma began his Test captaincy with a win against the West Indies in Centurion in February 2023. He won his next two matches as well before his team drew the third Test against the same opponents in Port of Spain in August 2024.His only defeat as Test captain came against Australia in Durban in October. Since then, South Africa have won three consecutive Tests under his leadership.Hassett began his captaincy career with a win against South Africa in Johannesburg in December 1949. Australia won the next two Tests under him before drawing the fourth match against the same opponents at the same venue in February 1950.His first defeat as captain came in his 10th Test, against England in Melbourne in February 1951. Hassett then led Australia to five consecutive wins before losing to South Africa in Melbourne in December 1952, in his 16th Test as captain.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Fanie de Villiers calls Usman Khawaja 'biggest traitor'; Cummins' captaincy faces threat as sandpaper shockwaves reverberate
articles.summary: Usman Khawaja has been called the “biggest traitor ever seen” by former South Africa captain Fanie de Villiers as the controversy surrounding Australia's
articles.body: Usman Khawaja has been called the “biggest traitor ever seen” by former South Africa captain Fanie de Villiers as the controversy surrounding Australia's ball-tampering scandal during the 2018 tour of South Africa continues to escalate.The latest developments have brought fresh scrutiny on several members of the Australian team, including Test captain Pat Cummins. The controversy resurfaced after Cameron Bancroft released a 4,000-word statement in which he made claims about his former teammates, including Cummins.While Cummins has faced calls to step down as Test captain, there has also been pressure on former coach Lehmann. Cricket Australia (CA) has announced that it will set up an independent forum where anyone involved can share information about the team's use of sandpaper to tamper the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.Khawaja has faced questions over why he waited eight years to say that the entire squad should take collective responsibility for the incident. Former Australia players Matthew Hayden and Ian Healy have also criticised him for discussing the matter publicly.De Villiers went further, questioning Khawaja's decision to bring the issue back into the public domain.“I want to go on record saying that Khawaja is probably the biggest traitor that I’ve ever seen in cricket that I’ve read in books and in cricket that I’ve seen over my last 40-50 years of watching the game,” he told 91.3 SportFM.“He’s broken every single code of conduct that one can think of. He’s sold out his players, fellow players."“This is not about right or wrong. The wrong has already been handled. It’s already been part of Australian cricket and it’s sad that it’s happened. But this guy has brought everything to the fore again. He’s brought Australian cricket into disrepute all over again. Breaking down of friendships. The code of conduct one has within the team," the former South African cricketer said.“He’s done everything wrong that one can think of."Mitchell Johnson believes Cummins may have to step downFormer Australia fast bowler Mitchell Johnson believes Cummins could struggle to continue as Test captain following the claims made by Bancroft and Khawaja. He also questioned whether the Australia skipper's public image could survive the controversy.Writing in a column for The West Australian, Johnson referred to his previous public disagreements with Cummins and said he believed Bancroft's account of the events.“I believe Bancroft’s account. It comes across as real and I could feel the words as he was saying them. He came across as himself and he has nothing to lose now. It also lines up with the most detailed accounts we’ve heard from other players,” Johnson wrote.Johnson said Cummins would come under pressure to step down, despite having stood by his earlier version of events.“The pressure on Cummins is now immense. I think he will still try to stand by what he has said and his statement with all of the bowlers back in 2021.“But I think the public pressure for Cummins to stand down as Test captain now will be too much. I just can’t see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this.“CA needs to do more than a safe-space forum. It’s owed to the fans, and they’ve had enough, like many of us. The investigation failed at the one thing it was meant to do, end this eight years ago with the right outcome. We want the truth, we want answers. But we also wish we had moved on all that time ago.”Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Observed a lot of things': Tilak Varma reveals how MS Dhoni, Rohit Sharma influenced his captaincy
articles.summary: Leadership is often shaped by observing the best, and India T20I vice-captain Tilak Varma is taking inspiration from two of Indian cricket's most
articles.body: Leadership is often shaped by observing the best, and India T20I vice-captain Tilak Varma is taking inspiration from two of Indian cricket's most successful leaders – MS Dhoni and Rohit Sharma. While he has never played under Dhoni, Tilak revealed that he has closely followed the former India captain's leadership style and regularly seeks his advice. However, when it comes to managing players and building relationships within a team, Rohit remains his biggest influence.Tilak is currently preparing to lead India A at the ACC Men's Rising Stars Asia Cup 2026 in Doha, Qatar. The 23-year-old will be entrusted with the responsibility of guiding a promising squad featuring Abhishek Sharma, Rinku Singh, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi and Harshit Rana.Speaking in a video shared by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) on Thursday, Tilak opened up about the leadership lessons he has picked up from some of India's most influential captains.Tilak Varma reveals what he has learnt from MS DhoniAlthough Tilak has played under Suryakumar Yadav, Rohit Sharma and Hardik Pandya, he has never had the opportunity to feature in a team led by Dhoni. Nevertheless, the youngster has closely observed the former India captain's approach to leadership and decision-making.Tilak revealed that he regularly interacts with Dhoni and has picked up several valuable lessons by watching how he manages different situations on the field.“I have played under Surya bhai, Rohit bhai, and Hardik bhai and observed a lot of things about Mahi bhai's captaincy. I have not played, but I have observed a lot of Mahi bhai's captaincy, and I talk to him a lot, and I have learnt a lot. Personally, I like to watch, and I have taken a lot of input from him, and I want to follow him and learn from him,” Tilak said.Rohit Sharma's man-management skills inspire TilakInterestingly, Tilak revealed that his conversations with Rohit are not always about batting, with the youngster more interested in understanding his approach to handling teammates, particularly during challenging situations.“I have learnt from Rohit bhai. I have seen him in MI and the Indian team. I always talk to him. I don't talk much about batting. Every player likes him. So I asked him, how do you take every player along with you? Off the field is the main role. So whatever he has done, I do it outside. I have my own way. I can take the player in my way when under pressure or in any situation,” he added.Tilak Varma-led India A begin Rising Stars Asia Cup campaign against NepalTilak will now look to put those leadership lessons into practice as India A begin their campaign at the Rising Stars Asia Cup. The 50-over tournament, which runs from November 19 to 29 in Doha, features eight teams divided into two groups.India A have been placed in Group B alongside Pakistan A, Nepal and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The top two teams from each group will progress to the semi-finals. India A will open their campaign against Nepal on November 20 before facing arch-rivals Pakistan A on November 22. Their final group-stage fixture will be against the UAE on November 24.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Bumrah or bust at the Basin: India err in team selection as New Zealand fight back from 70/5 to 243/5
articles.summary: The peerless Jasprit Bumrah could not have been happier when Indian captain Shubman Gill called correctly at the toss and opted to bowl first on a grassy
articles.body: The peerless Jasprit Bumrah could not have been happier when Indian captain Shubman Gill called correctly at the toss and opted to bowl first on a grassy Basin Reserve pitch on Thursday. After all, Bumrah had the equivalent of Australia’s famed pace trio of Mitchell Starc, Pat Cummins and Josh Hazlewood for company, capable of creating relentless pressure from the other end.After all, only a side blessed with a four-man pace attack of that potency and quality could afford to leave out Mohammed Siraj, India’s leading wicket-taker in the 2025-27 World Test Championship cycle with 43 scalps.Bumrah’s partners on Thursday were the profligate Prasidh Krishna, the military-medium Anshul Kamboj and the still-rusty Akash Deep. By stumps, when New Zealand had recovered from 70 for five to 243 for five through an unbroken 173-run partnership between Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips, the decision looked terribly flawed.The gulf in class between Bumrah and the rest of India’s pace attack became increasingly evident over the final two sessions as Nicholls and Phillips staged a remarkable rescue act. At stumps, Nicholls was unbeaten on 113 (221 balls) while Phillips was eyeing his second Test hundred on 94 (181).India will at least take the field on Friday with hope, as they have a ball that is still only two overs old.On Thursday, though, the visitors’ dominance appeared total. Gill’s decision to bowl first was vindicated immediately as Bumrah produced a masterclass with the new ball.Tom Latham shouldered arms to the fourth ball of the match only to see it jag back and clip off stump. It was the ninth time in his career that Bumrah had struck in his opening over. Devon Conway soon followed, driving loosely at Anshul Kamboj, while Akash Deep accounted for Rachin Ravindra after the batter had survived a missed DRS opportunity earlier.Daryl Mitchell, so often India’s tormentor, barely settled. Trying to negate the extra movement, he repeatedly used his feet in an attempt to disrupt Bumrah’s accuracy. The Indian spearhead responded brilliantly, shortening his length and angling one into the body. Mitchell felt cramped for room and was caught sharply by Yashasvi Jaiswal.When Tom Blundell, stuck at Bumrah’s end for 14 deliveries, edged him to first slip, New Zealand had slumped to 70 for five and India were on top.Challenging times, though, lay ahead.As the sun emerged, the surface eased and the Kookaburra lost its hardness. The green tinge gradually faded and India’s attack, lacking skill, pace and experience beyond Bumrah, became increasingly ineffective. While Bumrah continued to beat the bat, New Zealand found a generous release valve at the other end.Kamboj struggled to create sustained pressure. Operating below 130 kmph for most of the day, he neither hurried the batters nor extracted enough movement to threaten them. Prasidh Krishna repeatedly missed his lengths and the tactic of using him to bowl short from round the stumps looked odd as it was a pitch that demanded a good or fuller length.The pitch-map numbers indicated that. Deliveries on a good length yielded three wickets for 50 runs at an economy rate of 1.48. Balls bowled too full went for 67 runs, while short deliveries leaked 77 without producing a wicket.Nicholls, entrusted with the No. 3 position following Kane Williamson’s retirement, produced an innings of immense discipline and value. He left judiciously, trusted his defence and punished anything marginally overpitched.His hundred, reached off 188 balls, was his 12th in Test cricket and his fifth at Basin Reserve, drawing level with Martin Crowe and Williamson for centuries at the venue.On demanding surfaces, however, solidity alone is not enough. It must be complemented by energy and Phillips supplied exactly that. Fresh from a productive T20I series, the right-hander counter-attacked whenever India lacked control and turned the tide.The pair’s comfort levels at the crease were reflected in the numbers. Nicholls, playing late, registered a control percentage of 90.1 while Phillips was even more commanding at 91.8. By comparison, New Zealand’s other batters managed a collective control percentage of 69.5.India’s frustration compounded when Nicholls was offered a life after reaching his century. A miscued hook off Prasidh ballooned into the air, but confusion between Rishabh Pant running back and Devdutt Padikkal, who had called “mine”, at short square, meant the chance went abegging.The sixth-wicket stand also underlined India’s inability to finish off sides from dominant positions. It became the 31st partnership of 150-plus for the sixth wicket after a team had lost its first five wickets for fewer than 100 runs. India, sadly, have conceded six such stands.Unless Bumrah finds meaningful support on the second morning, New Zealand are well placed to turn a rescue mission into a match-defining first-innings advantage.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: IND vs NZ 1st Test: Popular or logical? India's team selection raises questions after Jadeja's shock exclusion
articles.summary: Ahead of the fifth T20I against New Zealand in Hamilton earlier this month, India head coach Gautam Gambhir told broadcasters: “My job is not to make
articles.body: Ahead of the fifth T20I against New Zealand in Hamilton earlier this month, India head coach Gautam Gambhir told broadcasters: “My job is not to make everyone happy. My job is to take the right decisions, not the popular decisions. The important thing is to make sure that there is a lot of security inside the dressing room.”Judging by India’s team combination for the first Test against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve, logic appears to have gone missing from the decision-making process as well.Leaving out Mohammed Siraj was one thing. Dropping Ravindra Jadeja was another.Siraj has been India’s leading wicket-taker in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle with 43 wickets. Jadeja is second on that list with 33. But Jadeja’s value extends well beyond his bowling.He is also India’s third-highest run-getter in this WTC cycle, scoring 790 runs in 11 matches at an average of 60.76. The last time India toured outside the subcontinent, in England in 2025, Jadeja amassed 516 runs in five Tests at an average of 86.His wicket-taking threat may not be what it once was, but he remains a world-class holding bowler and arguably India’s most dependable all-round cricketer. On Day One at Wellington, Washington Sundar performed a containing role. Jadeja could have done that too, while offering significantly more with the bat.As Sunil Gavaskar remarked on commentary: “If you did not want to play him, being such a senior cricketer, why bring him here?”Did Sundar play ahead of Jadeja because New Zealand’s top four comprise left-handers and the management wanted an off-spinner capable of turning the ball away from them?Explaining the call after stumps, batting coach Sitanshu Kotak confirmed: “We preferred Washy as their top order had four left-handers.”The problem with that argument is that Jadeja has built a career troubling left-handers.Of his 356 Test wickets, 120 have been left-handed batters dismissed at an average of 25.75. Among his regular victims are Ben Stokes (eight times), Moeen Ali (seven), Alastair Cook (seven), Matthew Wade (five), David Warner (four) and Usman Khawaja (four).If such a stellar record doesn’t inspire confidence against left-handers, what exactly does?Speaking on his YouTube channel, former India off-spinner R Ashwin questioned the rationale behind leaving out Jadeja."Left-handers often struggle against left-arm spinners because of the rough that develops outside off stump. Just as left-arm pacers create rough for off-spinners to exploit, this Test features eight right-arm seamers across both teams, most of whom will bowl over the wicket and create rough outside the left-hander's off stump for Jadeja. In overseas Tests, a spinner's primary role usually comes into play on Days Four and Five. If Washington Sundar is playing, he is effectively replacing a batter. Jadeja, on the other hand, walks into the side on pure merit. He has been India's best overseas batter over the last couple of years," Ashwin stressed.There also seems to be confusion about how India view Nitish Kumar Reddy.The team management has repeatedly spoken about grooming him as a pace-bowling all-rounder for overseas conditions. He was pulled out of the ODI series after the first match and rushed from Auckland to Wellington to prepare for the Tests.Yet when the opportunity arrived, in favourable conditions, he wasn’t picked.This brings us back to Gambhir’s comments about creating security within the dressing room.Players understand being dropped for poor form or when conditions demand a different combination. What they struggle to understand is when messaging of the management and their actions don’t align.If Reddy is genuinely part of India’s long-term overseas plans, shouldn’t he be getting game time? If Jadeja remains one of India’s premier allrounders, why is he sitting out? If Siraj is your leading wicket-taker in the WTC cycle, what exactly was the logic behind excluding him on a green Wellington pitch?Popular decisions don’t always have to be right. But right decisions, at the very least, should be logical.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Just the second batter in history of cricket! Glenn Phillips equals Rohit Sharma's rare feat with century against India
articles.summary: New Zealand batter Glenn Phillips became the first player to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India in the same
articles.body: New Zealand batter Glenn Phillips became the first player to score centuries in all three formats of international cricket against India in the same calendar year. He achieved the milestone on Day 2 of the first Test at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Friday.Phillips completed his century in the first innings of the ongoing Test, having already scored hundreds against India in ODIs and T20Is earlier this year. He scored 106 in the ODI at Indore on January 18 before hitting 107 off 49 balls in the T20I at Auckland on October 30.He is the second player overall to score a century in Tests, ODIs and T20Is against the same opponent in a calendar year. Former India captain Rohit Sharma was the first to achieve the feat, scoring centuries against Sri Lanka in all three formats in 2017.Phillips also became the first New Zealand batter to score centuries against the same opponent across all three formats. Batting at No. 7 in the first innings of the Wellington Test, he took 194 deliveries to reach the three-figure mark.Hundreds against a team in all three formats in a calendar yearRohit Sharma vs Sri Lanka in 2017Glenn Phillips vs India in 2026Overall, Phillips is the third player, after Australia's Shane Watson and West Indies batter Shai Hope, to score centuries against India in all three international formats.Phillips was eventually dismissed for 118 when Akash Deep bowled him in the 94th over. The India seamer beat the batter with a delivery that moved away and hit the top of the off stump.Phillips has now scored centuries in consecutive Tests, having made exactly 100 in New Zealand's 253-run win over England at The Oval in June. He has also scored centuries for New Zealand in all three formats.His dismissal brought an end to a 216-run partnership with Henry Nicholls, which began in the 29th over, shortly after lunch on Day 1.Nicholls continued New Zealand's innings after the break and reached his 150 shortly after lunch on Day 2. At the time of writing, New Zealand were 348/8 after 116 overs.FOLLOW LIVEGet the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Mohammed Siraj, victim of a communication breakdown?
articles.summary: Fifteen months ago, on a cloudy London morning, Mohammed Siraj emerged from Jasprit Bumrah’s shadow.
articles.body: Fifteen months ago, on a cloudy London morning, Mohammed Siraj emerged from Jasprit Bumrah’s shadow. Despite a battered body, Siraj summoned enough belief on the final day of a gruelling five-Test series to deliver India’s finest moment in Test cricket since the Gabba win of 2021.He emptied the tank to secure a 2-2 scoreline for India at the Oval and it seemed to mark the beginning of a new phase — Siraj was ready to lead India’s attack as Bumrah entered an intensive workload management programme.On Thursday, in conditions tailor-made for seam bowling, Siraj was not considered for India’s fourpronged pace attack in Wellington. One might point to his uninspiring performance against Sri Lanka in the Colombo Test three months ago as the moment the team management began to question his ability.However, things had started to simmer when he asked for a break from the two T20Is in Ireland after the one-off Test against Afghanistan in June. Subsequently, communication channels began to break down as he was omitted from the white-ball team in the summer.The team management was reportedly unhappy that he barely bowled during the two-month break. That was identified as the reason his pace dropped to the early 120-125 kmph range in Sri Lanka. The selectors and team management were still reassessing his role across formats when he was suddenly asked to report to the CoE during UK’s white-ball tour.Over the last month, Siraj has been all over the place — domestic cricket, the CoE, the India ‘A’ team and the ODI team in New Zealand, in stark contrast to the others’ meticulously planned preparations.Siraj is a player who feeds off the confidence shown in him. With him, that can happen only through frequent conversations. Anyone who has worked with him will testify to how difficult it is to ask him to slow down. Perhaps the caretakers of Indian cricket could at least try to understand why someone of his character asked for a breather.“You have to have regular conversations with Siraj. He has an uncomplicated mind. If you constantly have those discussions with him, he understands the nuances of high-performance sport. And he becomes the man who can go to any lengths for you,” India’s previous bowling coach Paras Mhambrey, who also worked with Siraj during his India ‘A’ days, told TOI.“I can’t comment on whether the team management observed anything wrong, but Siraj still has a good three years of Test cricket left. He is experienced enough to understand how much bowling he needs to do to stay in rhythm. He has developed very well as a successor to Bumrah in the 48 Tests he played,” Mhambrey said.“His experience and ability to come hard at the batsmen all day also help manage Bumrah’s workload. Siraj seemed to be hitting good speeds during the IPL and even in the last ODI he played. It’s about sitting him down and explaining the road ahead,” he added.The confusion around Siraj is evident. Batting coach Sitanshu Kotak was at his most defiant that the management was not wrong to bench Siraj. Amid all this, the road ahead for India’s most experienced pacer after Bumrah looks rough.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Australia captain Pat Cummins found himself surrounded by reporters outside his home on Thursday as questions about the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal resurfaced.The incident returned to the headlines after former Australia batter Cameron Bancroft claimed that the entire team knew about the ball-tampering incident, contradicting Cummins' recent statement that he had no knowledge of it.A video of the incident has gone viral on social media, showing Cummins being approached by several journalists as he appeared to leave for training. When one reporter apologised for entering his premises, the Australian captain responded sharply, saying, "You're probably not that sorry".Cummins refused to answer questions about Bancroft's allegations, including whether he felt his former teammate had thrown him under the bus and whether the controversy could put his captaincy at risk. He maintained his silence, got into his car and drove away.Watch:Bancroft claims entire team knew about SandpapergateThe fresh controversy began after Bancroft published a detailed account of the 2018 scandal in Australian newspaper The West Australian. He claimed that the ball-tampering incident was not limited to himself, Steve Smith and David Warner, but that the entire team was aware of what was happening."It was not just the three of us, Steve Smith, David Warner and I, who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote.He also claimed that he regularly spoke to Australia's fast bowlers, including Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, about whether the ball was reverse-swinging properly.Bancroft says Cummins' statement hurt himBancroft revealed that Cummins' recent press conference was the main reason he decided to share his account publicly.He said the Australian captain's denial left him feeling hurt after carrying the burden of the incident for years."But the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference. articles.title: 50/4 and a lot of heat: How Akash Deep sparked India's turnaround on Day 2
articles.summary: Wellington: The Basin Reserve pitch blended with the outfield in its lushness when both India and New Zealand were putting the finishing touches to their
articles.body: Wellington: The Basin Reserve pitch blended with the outfield in its lushness when both India and New Zealand were putting the finishing touches to their preparations. It had a considerable tinge on the opening day too, but as the players took the field for the second day, the surface started turning brown as the 15mm grass cover took on a burnt look on another sunny morning. The handful of trees circling the ground remained still as the notorious Welly Wind stayed at bay, suggesting another day of chasing leather for the Indian cricket team.The visitors tried a few different things from the first delivery, hoping to break the frustrating 216-run partnership between Henry Nicholls and Glenn Phillips for the sixth wicket. Jasprit Bumrah changed ends, and Prasidh Krishna shared the second new ball with him. The pitch, however, had now lost its opening-day morning sting and looked rather comfortable for batting. The experiment didn't last long as Prasidh continued to bowl erratic lines, and Bumrah couldn't find the rhythm he enjoyed when bowling from the scoreboard end.India sought wickets, but both Nicholls and Phillips looked rock-solid until Akash Deep produced a peach to dismiss Phillips shortly after he scored a brilliant hundred. Angled in, shaping away and hitting the top of the stumps is every fast bowler's delight, and Akash was pumped. The moment lifted the Indian team, which had been very flat during the mammoth stand, and they had their tails up for the remainder of the innings.Akash looked very good, and Bumrah continued doing Bumrah things as India wasted very little time picking up the remaining four wickets. The lower order and the tail have been India's nemesis in the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, but that wasn't the case on Friday. The last four wickets added just 30 runs, and New Zealand collapsed from 318/6 to 368 all out.On either side of the 216-run stand between Nicholls and Phillips, India can be pleased with their efforts of 70/5 and 50/4. Had India found a way through when the left-right combination kept them wicketless for over five hours, it could well have been a different story for the visitors. Except for the dropped catch late on the opening day, Nicholls looked in absolute control during his unbeaten 175 off 335 balls.The left-hander enjoyed a very strong control percentage and improved his average at this venue to 91.5. He had in-form Phillips for company for most of his innings, and the right-hander became only the second player to hit hundreds across formats against the same team in a single year. Rohit Sharma achieved the rare feat back in 2017 against Sri Lanka.New Zealand have 368 on the board, and India will be mighty pleased with how they responded after the hosts' defiance in the morning session. If not for some disciplined bowling post-Lunch, it could have been much worse for Shubman Gill & Co. Over to the batters now.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: IPL has fast-tracked New Zealand cricket’s rise: Ross Taylor
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Ross Talyor has been keenly watching the first Test match between India and New Zealand which began on Thursday at Wellington.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Ross Talyor has been keenly watching the first Test match between India and New Zealand which began on Thursday at Wellington."I think India did well. five for 70, I think they would have found they were in a good position. Henry Nicholls, obviously India have got the new ball, the second new ball tomorrow. And they'll be wanting to take some early wickets. I thought (Jasprit) Bumrah bowled outstandingly well. And it wasn't as green as it normally is in Wellington. I think it browned off pretty quickly after lunch. So I'm sure the Indian batters will want to get through that new ball tomorrow. And if they can do that, we'll look forward to batting on a flat wicket," former New Zealand batter RossTaylor told TOI on Thursday in an exclusive interview at the ProWine event here at the Jio Convention Centre Centre on Thursday.Talking about the New Zealand cricket team's transformation over the last two decades, Taylor said, "From here, I think it's probably a good summation of where we were as a team. And where we are. Today is chalk and cheese from that. We've got some world-class players now. The likes of (Daniel) Vettori, (Bendon) McCullum, (Tim) Southee, (Trent) Bolt, (Kane) Williamson. I think when you have world-class players on your team, you bring everyone else with you. And I think the standards have gone up. And I think probably the IPL has played a part in that too in having New Zealand players learn and rub shoulders with the best players in the world has, I think, fast-tracked their learning as well."What has been the biggest cultural shift in New Zealand cricket during his playing career you are tempted to ask Taylor. "I think when you have world-class players, the other players have to lift. I think the culture has been great. And I think the.continuation of the team has just got better and better," he said.The Blacks Caps have earned a reputation for consistency and humility under Kane Williamson. How much of that culture was built over the years by players like yourself, Ben McCullum and Daniel Vittori? “I think you'd have to ask the other players that. I think New Zealand, as nature, are pretty reserved and humble people. We want to go out there and play hard cricket, but there's still a way to play hard cricket, but play in the spirit of the game as well,” Taylor said.Does he think New Zealand has maximized its talent pool or there's still untapped potential in the system? "Yes, I think probably a bit of both. I think the team is growing quickly. We've got some good young players coming through. There's always a transition period and the players are getting older, so I think the New Zealand team needs to get a few more youngsters in. Ratchin's (Ravindra) come in and had success, but hopefully we can get some other players. I think we've got some good bowlers coming through, but hopefully some young batters can come through in the next couple of years,” saidHow challenging has it been for New Zealand to manage the transition as senior players retire? “That's what I mean. I think that's going to be the key going forward. Just the way the international schedule works, the World Cup plays a big part, so those senior players like to work towards World Cups and quite often retire after that. Once the next World Cup comes around, I think it's a time for New Zealand cricket and probably a lot of other countries to rebuild their teams,” felt Taylor, at Pro Wine 2026 here on Thursday.Having played alongside former New Zealand captain Kane Williamson for so long, the one quality people outside the dressing room don't fully appreciate, according to Tayor is, "I think he's a great cricketer and a world-class person, and that shows on the cricket field, but that is who he is. I think a lot of players are different from what they are on the field, is what you see from Kane is what you get from him.”Talking about how he was going about his business of Pro Wines, Taylor said, "It's good to be here at Pro Wines Mumbai as an ambassador for the New Zealand pavilion. If you would have said to me when I retired a few years ago that I'd be in the wine industry, I would have said absolutely no chance. But it's been great to be here and obviously with the New Zealand Free Trade Agreement with India, I think it's a good chance for the two countries that we have strong relationships in a sporting context, but bringing it together in a business capacity will just keep going from strength to strength.”Talking about what separates Virat Kohli from other modern greats in the ODI format, Taylor said, "They'll (Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli) will be there at that World Cup. They're still fit as ever and just their catches that they took in that series, they might have not scored the amount of runs that they would have liked, their athleticism,till there at and 40 and I'm sure for the Indian crowd and, going out there and watching them for their last time, which I hope it's not their last time, but obviously it's getting towards the end of their career and for all cricket fans around the world, hopefully they can play for a bit longer," Taylor concluded.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
